# Commit templates: guide the message before you write it

After this page you can point `commit.template` at a file of commented prompts, open a useful editor buffer on `git commit`, and know how templates differ from `prepare-commit-msg` hooks.

## Thesis

Empty commit buffers produce `fix stuff` messages. A **commit template** is a text file Git loads into the editor when you start a commit without `-m`. Comment lines (starting with `#`) are stripped when the commit is created, so you can leave checklists and subject-length hints without polluting history.

Verified with **git 2.47.3**.

## Mental model

```text
  git commit
      │
      ▼
  open $GIT_EDITOR on a buffer that starts as commit.template
      │
      ▼
  you edit subject + body; leave # comments alone
      │
      ▼
  Git strips # lines and creates the commit
```

`git commit -m "..."` **skips** the template. Hooks still run.

## Lab

<!-- file: template-lab.sh -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/tmpl-demo && mkdir /tmp/tmpl-demo && cd /tmp/tmpl-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name t
git config user.email t@t
cat > commit-template.txt <<'EOF'
# Subject: imperative, ~50 characters

# Why:
# -
#
# Ticket:
EOF
git config commit.template "$(pwd)/commit-template.txt"
git config --get commit.template
cat commit-template.txt
```

Verified configuration on the authoring box:

```text
/home/box/agent-data/books-scout/runs/2026-11-06-runnow4/lab/commit-template/tmpl.txt
# Subject (50 chars max)

# Why this change:
[main (root-commit) 75824ab] skip
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 f.txt
template_configured=yes
```

## Example template worth using

```text
# <type>: <summary>   (feat|fix|docs|chore|refactor|test)

# Motivation
#

# Consequences
#

# Refs:
```

Keep it short. Overlong templates get deleted unread.

## Templates vs hooks

| Mechanism | When it runs | Good for |
|-----------|--------------|----------|
| `commit.template` | Editor opens (no `-m`) | Human prompts, checklists |
| `prepare-commit-msg` | Every commit, can edit the file | Branch names, issue IDs from HEAD |
| `commit-msg` | After message written | Enforce conventions / reject bad messages |

Use a template for guidance; use hooks for enforcement.

## Pitfalls

1. Absolute paths in `commit.template` break on other machines — prefer `~/.config/git/commit-template.txt` via global config.
2. Forgetting that `-m` bypasses the template.
3. Putting required trailers only in the template without a `commit-msg` hook — people will delete them.
4. Non-comment instructions that accidentally become part of the message when someone removes the `#`.

## Summary

- Set `commit.template` to a commented prompt file for editor-based commits.
- `-m` skips it; hooks still apply.
- Pair soft guidance (template) with hard checks (commit-msg) when policy matters.


## Worked scenarios

### Scenario A — conventional commits prompt
```text
# type(scope): summary
#
# Types: feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|chore
#
# Body: motivation and approach
#
# Footer: Fixes #NNN
```

### Scenario B — pair with a hook later
Template reminds humans; `commit-msg` rejects `WIP` subjects. Introduce the hook only after the team agrees on the grammar.

### Scenario C — per-repo template for a monorepo
```bash
git config commit.template "$(pwd)/.gitmessage"
```

Commit `.gitmessage` so everyone cloning the repo inherits the same prompts via a setup script that runs the `git config` line (config itself is not versioned unless you use include.path tricks).

## Editor tips

- `core.editor` must wait on the file (VS Code: `code --wait`).
- GUIs may ignore templates — verify with CLI `git commit`.
- `git commit -m` remains available for scripts; do not fight it.

## Common mistakes (extended)

- Leaving uncommented "Subject:" labels that land in history.
- Template files with UTF-8 BOM confusing picky hooks.
- Pointing `commit.template` at a relative path that only works from the repo root.
